open_assumptions: A double forfeit is represented as winner -1 with reason 'forfeit'. No new end reason was added and PROTOCOL_VERSION is unchanged. The standalone duel room has no rewards, so 'rewards cancelled' only means that no winner is recorded (documented in docs/duel.md).

The same-frame double-forfeit integration test drops both players for real, then calls DuelRoom.onLeave for both seats in one synchronous block, in each order. This is what Colyseus does when both reconnection timers fire in the same tick. Real timers are not forced onto one frame.
Prediction now also stops at a predicted result, not only a confirmed one, and resumes if a correction takes the result back (unit-tested). This changes the shared rollback core's behaviour.
The duel gate's rate window now starts at tick 0 like the world gate's, instead of at the first message. This only changes the first second of a room.
ArenaFlashes keeps its own memory of the last 64 ids on top of DuelEventFeed's de-duplication.

findings.message: apps/web/src/devLatency.ts DelayLine.push keeps order only on paper. It clamps each item's due time to the previous item's (`at = max(last, now + delay)`), then schedules every item with its own `setTimeout(deliver, at - now)`. Two clamped items share the same `at`, but real timers do not fire them in push order. In Node, the timer expiry is libuv-now (whole ms, cached per loop turn) plus the fractional delay. So when two messages are pushed in the same loop turn (for example two WebSocket frames from one read) and the second is clamped, the second gets the strictly earlier expiry and fires first. In the browser, WebIDL truncates the delay to whole ms, so a clamped item fires first whenever its fractional offset is smaller, which is about half of clamped pairs spaced more than 1 ms apart. The unit tests use vitest fake timers, which order by exact time and then insertion, so they cannot see this. The acceptance clause that the dev latency tests fail when ordering breaks therefore holds only under fake timers. At ?rtt=80&jitter=20 the effect is mostly harmless reordering between different message kinds (a bundle against a patch or probe). With larger jitter, or after a main-thread stall that batches arrivals, it reorders frame bundles, which the rollback treats as a gap and waits for a snapshot to fix, and it can reorder Colyseus state patches. That distorts the operator's playtest, the one thing this setting exists for. Fix: use one FIFO queue per direction drained by a single timer, as packages/test-tools/src/impairmentProxy.ts Pipe already does.
findings.requirement: delay outgoing and incoming messages, probes included, by about RTT/2 each way, add bounded jitter, and never reorder

findings.message: apps/web/src/duel.test.ts:284-321 ('delays the room's socket both ways...') tests only the base delay for the outgoing path of applyDevLatency. The shared draw list [0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.999999, 0] gives both outgoing messages (the probe echo and the input) a draw of 0.5, which means zero jitter, and they are sent 40 ms apart, so they could never reorder. Only the incoming bundles use extreme draws. The DelayLine unit tests (lines 211-263) do cover the jitter bound and ordering, but a regression in the wrapper's send side would pass every test: a DelayLine per send, a plain setTimeout, or an outgoing line built without jitter. The integration test would not catch it either, because redundant inputs mask stale-sequence drops. Suggested fix: send two outgoing messages a few ms apart with draws 0.999999 then 0, and assert that they leave in order at the jitter bounds.
findings.requirement: delay outgoing and incoming messages, probes included, by about RTT/2 each way, add bounded jitter, and never reorder

# Decisions: duel-online-fixes

From the operator session of 2026-09-24, written by the assistant under the operator's standing instruction to keep the slices moving. Run duel-online-001 passed every check, but its coverage reviewer blocked the candidate (P1: the dev latency setting's behaviour is untested) and its general reviewer was stopped before a verdict.

## Decisions

- As with `world-sea-fixes`, the follow-up starts from the run's base (`b8c2934`, branch `duel-online/base`) and restores its snapshot (`cb8fe85`, `refs/workflow/9d324071c360f7c2/duel`) as its first step, so the new reviewers see the whole combat spike plus the fixes. No general review of it was ever completed.
- The dev latency setting is proven below the browser: unit tests with fake timers, plus an integration test that wraps a headless duel client in the same module. The browser checks run the production build, where the setting is absent by design, and adding a dev-server browser run would add a port and a slow build for little gain.
- Scope: the coverage reviewer's P1 and four P2s, and three P2s from the assistant's review.
- §12 forfeits, corrected after design challenge attempt 1. The assistant first asked for a broad "both absent → cancel" rule; the challenge showed that misreads §12, because a player whose window expires while the opponent is still within theirs forfeits as normal. §12 cancels rewards only when both forfeit on the same tick. The rule is now spec-literal: forfeits are evaluated together at the frame boundary, and only simultaneous expiries cancel, so processing order can't invent a winner (§7).
- Timing assertions follow the challenge's advice. Exact input-delay values are unit-tested on the pure selection function; live tests assert only banded, relative facts (delayed > undelayed, within 3..8).
- The task tells the worker never to stop processes by name pattern. duel-online-001's `pkill -f vite` killed another run's `vitest` on this shared machine.
- The same lane, owned paths, checks and scenario ids as `duel-online`.

## Assumptions

- The assistant's review of the snapshot found no P0 or P1. It reran integration 32/32 in about 102 s. The harness reached 0 desyncs over 181/181 hash checks and 0 rate-limited drops at both no impairment and 80 ms / 20 ms / 1 %.
- Merging with `main` (which now has `claim-channel` and `objectives-ledger`) has two additive conflicts (the simulation `exports` block and `scripts/smoke-build.ts`), which the assistant resolves by keeping every entry.

## Deferred

- The spike's exit, the operator's playtest at §19's latencies, follows this run.
- The same "both forfeit on the same tick" gap in `objectives-ledger`'s quit path: a later fix to the ledger.
- Tuning the input-delay policy after the playtest.

concerns.message: Finding 2 makes the harness assert that the input delay at 80 ms / 20 ms / 1 % is strictly greater than at no impairment. duel-online-001 only printed `inputDelay`, and neither the task nor decisions.md records the two values. If the snapshot's selection policy returns the same delay for both (for example the floor of 3, because 40 ms one-way is under 3 frames), the assertion cannot pass without retuning the policy, and decisions.md defers that tuning until after the playtest.
concerns.consequence: The worker finds out mid-run that the required live assertion fails. It then either retunes the deferred policy on its own or reports blocked. The same risk applies in reverse if the no-impairment run on the shared machine measures a spike, which makes 'greater than' flaky.

concerns.message: Finding 6's 'same duel frame' is only deterministic if each forfeit deadline is stored as a frame on the room's tick counter (leave frame + 600) and the room decides expiry at the frame boundary. The alternative is to keep Colyseus's wall-clock `allowReconnection(client, 10)` timers and queue their rejections for the next tick. Then 'same frame' depends on setTimeout jitter and event-loop lag on a shared machine: two drops a few ms apart may or may not merge. The deadline also has to count on a counter that advances during the countdown, not only on the duel simulation frame, or a drop during the countdown never expires.
concerns.consequence: The both-forfeit cancel case behaves nondeterministically in production, and an integration test for it flakes. That is exactly the order-dependence §7 and §12 forbid.

concerns.message: Finding 1 imports `apps/web/src/devLatency.ts` from `tests/integration`. The root `tsconfig.json` includes `tests/**/*.ts` with `types: ["node"]` and nodenext resolution, but not `vite/client`. Every file devLatency.ts pulls in (transitively) is therefore typechecked under the root config.
concerns.consequence: If devLatency.ts or anything it imports reads `import.meta.env` or depends on Vite/DOM-only types, `npm run typecheck` fails. The URL/env gate has to stay in the caller (duel.ts/main.ts), and devLatency.ts should depend only on the SDK room/transport types.

concerns.message: Finding 7 assumes the client is behind the final frame when the phase becomes 'over'. With prediction the client may already be ahead of the terminal frame, and the server may not send a bundle that ends exactly on the KO or timeout frame, because bundles go out on a 3-frame cadence and the result is a separate message. 'Keep stepping' alone does not reach the confirmed final state in either case.
concerns.consequence: The HUD shows predicted health or clock past the KO, or stops 1–2 frames short, unless the server sends a final bundle with a snapshot at the terminal frame and the client restores to that frame.

concerns.message: Finding 3's browser stamina check after a dash has a short window: the dash costs 20, regeneration starts after 1 s, and stamina is back at 100 about 2 s later. Adding the dash in the middle of `duel-practice` also moves the fighter, which can break the jab and throw range the scenario depends on.
concerns.consequence: A flaky or broken existing scenario (`duel-practice`/`duel-online`). Add the dash after the existing assertions, and poll for a value below 100 (or exactly 80) soon after the dash, not at a fixed time.

concerns.message: The new integration cases add time to a suite measured at about 102 s. The dev-latency test needs a countdown with and without delay (unless it reuses a baseline), and each forfeit case needs a real 10 s absence. The integration project's default test timeout is 20 s.
concerns.consequence: This still fits in 300 s, but only if the both-forfeit case is unit-tested on a pure resolver rather than run live. Otherwise the suite gets slower and more timing-sensitive on the shared machine.

challenge.simpler_alternative: Handle findings 6 and 7 with pure, frame-deterministic code instead of timing live sockets. For 6, keep a forfeit deadline frame per player on the room's tick counter, use Colyseus 'manual' reconnection so no wall-clock timer decides, and call a pure `resolveForfeits(deadlines, frame)` once per tick. That function returns 'none', 'one forfeits' or 'both forfeit, cancel rewards'. Unit-test all three outcomes, and keep a single live integration test for the ordinary one-player forfeit, which already exists. For 7, have the server always send a final bundle with a snapshot at the terminal frame. On 'over', the client restores that confirmed state rather than stepping forward. It cannot overshoot the KO, and the unit test is simple.
challenge.cheap_experiment: Before any worker starts, read duel-online-001's integration output (or rerun only the harness test at the snapshot, about 1 minute) and compare the printed `inputDelay` at no impairment with the one at 80/20/1. At the same time, run `git show cb8fe85:apps/server/src/DuelRoom.ts` to see how reconnection deadlines and the countdown tick are implemented. If both delays are equal, the 'delayed > undelayed' assertion needs a policy decision now (retune, or assert only in the dev-latency test with a larger latency). If the deadlines are wall-clock timers, finding 6 needs frame deadlines as described above.

# Task: duel

## Goal

Deliver the `duel-online` combat spike with its review findings fixed. Run duel-online-001 built it and passed every check: 32 integration tests, and a harness at 80 ms / 20 ms / 1 % with 0 desyncs over 181 hash checks and 0 rate-limited drops. But its coverage reviewer blocked the candidate, because nothing tests the dev latency setting the operator's playtest depends on, and its general reviewer never finished. Start from that run's snapshot, then close the findings below so that the whole feature can be reviewed again.

## Context

- `features/duel-online/duel-task.md` and `features/duel-online/decisions.md` define the feature, and all of it still applies. Read them first.
- **First step:** restore duel-online-001's snapshot (commit `cb8fe85`) into your worktree, deletions included, but not `features/`:
  `git restore --source=refs/workflow/9d324071c360f7c2/duel --staged --worktree -- . ':!features'`.
  `git restore` works in no-overlay mode, so it also removes files the snapshot deleted, which `git checkout <ref> -- .` would leave behind. Check with `git diff --stat refs/workflow/9d324071c360f7c2/duel -- . ':!features'` (empty). The restore changes only paths this lane owns. Then read `docs/duel.md` and `docs/architecture.md`.
- The verifier runs `npm ci`, then `npm run typecheck`, `npm run test:unit`, `npm run test:integration`, `npm run build` and `npx --no-install playwright test --config=tests/e2e/playwright.config.ts`. Playwright's Chromium for `@playwright/test` 1.63.0 is installed and shared read-only; never run `playwright install`.
- Other features (`claim-channel`, `objectives-ledger`) are already on `main` and will be merged with this one afterwards. Don't recreate them here.
- **This machine is shared by several runs. Never stop processes by name pattern (`pkill -f`, `killall`, and so on): `pkill -f vite` also matched another run's `vitest` and failed its verification. Stop only the PIDs you started.**

Findings to fix (coverage reviewer unless noted):

1. (P1) The dev latency setting's behaviour has no test. `apps/web/src/duel.test.ts` only parses the query, and the smoke check only proves the setting is absent from the production bundle. The browser checks run that production build, so prove the behaviour below the browser:
   - unit tests (fake timers) show that `applyDevLatency` / `DelayLine` (`apps/web/src/devLatency.ts`) delay outgoing and incoming messages, probes included, by about RTT/2 each way, add bounded jitter, and never reorder;
   - an integration test wraps a headless duel client's transport in that same module (import it from `apps/web/src`; keep it free of DOM dependencies so Node can load it) and shows that the room's measured round trip and its chosen input delay rise above the no-latency case.
2. (P2) Nothing asserts that input-delay selection follows measured latency; the harness only prints `inputDelay`.
   - Unit-test the pure selection function (RTT and jitter samples → frames) for exact values.
   - In live tests (the harness and the dev-latency integration test), assert only banded, relative facts: the delay under impairment is greater than the delay without it, and both are within 3..8. Live sockets on a shared machine can't give exact values.
3. (P2) The HUD's stamina display (`apps/web/src/duelHud.ts`) is never read by a test. Assert it in a browser scenario (for example after a dash) and in a unit test.
4. (P2, keep it in pure netcode unit tests) The resync-after-stall test (`packages/simulation/src/netcode/netcode.test.ts`) ends with `expect(bundle).toBeDefined()` and never checks the restored state. Assert that the session's confirmed state equals the authority's after `resync()`. Add the case the requirement names: contiguous bundles keep arriving while ticks stall, as in a hidden tab.
5. (P2, keep it in pure netcode and view unit tests) Stable-id de-duplication is tested only for a hit at the rollback level. Add a KO re-simulated by a correction, and a view-side test showing that the arena and the client's pending-event buffer show each event once.
6. (P2, assistant's review, corrected by design challenge attempt 1) Implement §12 literally.
   - When one player's 10-second window expires while the other is connected, or still inside their own window, that player forfeits and the other wins, as the snapshot already does. Keep it.
   - When both expiries resolve on the **same duel frame**, neither player wins and unresolved rewards are cancelled ("both forfeit on the same tick"). Evaluate forfeits together at the frame boundary, so that processing order can never invent a winner (§7). Today the first `onLeave` (`apps/server/src/DuelRoom.ts`, around lines 181–184) decides by order.
   - Unit- or integration-test both cases.
7. (P2, assistant's review) When the phase becomes "over", the client stops ticking (`apps/web/src/duelClient.ts`, around line 129), so the HUD's result, clock and health can trail the final bundle. Keep stepping to the last bundle's frame, with a hard stop at the final confirmed frame, so it never predicts past the KO or the timeout.
8. (P2, assistant's review) `DuelInputGate` copies the world `InputGate`'s rate and validation logic. Share it (for example a common rate window) so they cannot drift, keeping `InputGate`'s behaviour and tests unchanged.

## Constraints

- Owned paths as in `policy.json`. Apart from restoring the snapshot, change only what the findings need, and keep the existing structure, names and patterns.
- The duel rules stay untouched, as in `features/duel-online/duel-task.md`. Keep the protocol version, the six browser scenario ids and every existing test.
- Tests drive input like players do.

## Acceptance

- The restored `duel-online` feature meets all of `features/duel-online/duel-task.md`'s acceptance.
- Findings 1–8 are fixed with the tests they name. The dev latency tests fail if the delay, the jitter bound or the ordering breaks. The input-delay assertions fail if the chosen delay ignores measured latency.
- The integration suite stays well inside its 300-second check timeout.
- `npm ci` then each of the five policy checks passes from a clean checkout.

Browser checks: each scenario id appears in exactly one test title as `[scenario:<id>]`. That test, when it passes, attaches exactly one image/png named `screenshot:<id>` (other attachments are fine). The verifier refuses anything else. Before completing, run the spec files you changed with a JSON report:

```bash
WORKFLOW_VERIFICATION_PHASE=worker PLAYWRIGHT_JSON_OUTPUT_FILE=<tmp>/report.json \
  npx --no-install playwright test --config=tests/e2e/playwright.config.ts --reporter=json <spec files>
```

Then check the report with the verifier's own rules: run the exact `check-report` command the controller appends to this task when it pins it.

## Stop

Report `blocked` instead of continuing when any of these happens:

- Restoring the snapshot fails or touches a path outside the owned paths.
- `npm ci` or an install fails twice for reasons outside the repository (registry, network).
- A check can pass only by changing a path outside the owned paths.
- After two hours of work, any required check still fails and you cannot name the next fix.

Report `question` only for a choice that would change this acceptance.

open_assumptions: A double forfeit is represented as winner -1 with reason 'forfeit'. No new end reason was added and PROTOCOL_VERSION is unchanged. The standalone duel room has no rewards, so 'rewards cancelled' only means that no winner is recorded (documented in docs/duel.md).

The same-frame double-forfeit integration test drops both players for real, then calls DuelRoom.onLeave for both seats in one synchronous block, in each order. This is what Colyseus does when both reconnection timers fire in the same tick. Real timers are not forced onto one frame.
Prediction now also stops at a predicted result, not only a confirmed one, and resumes if a correction takes the result back (unit-tested). This changes the shared rollback core's behaviour.
The duel gate's rate window now starts at tick 0 like the world gate's, instead of at the first message. This only changes the first second of a room.
ArenaFlashes keeps its own memory of the last 64 ids on top of DuelEventFeed's de-duplication.
